newsitem.title: UK: Coffee chief says growers hold the price key now.
newsitem.headline: Coffee chief says growers hold the price key now.

text.p: Growers hold the key to coffee prices now that reserves in consumer nations have been drained, the head of the International Coffee Organization (ICO) said on Wednesday.
"All the elements are in the hands of the producers...The farmers will dictate the pace of everything," Celsius Lodder, ICO executive director, told Reuters in an interview.
"Before, the supplies were in the hands of the roasters, stocks were at very high levels, then it changed...That's part of the game."
"Now you have more influential behaviour from the growers than from the roasters," he said.
The ICO groups 62 coffee exporting and consumer nations. It is to meet in London next week. Members account for 97 percent of world supply.
Lodder's comments were made against a backdrop of surging coffee futures, on the back of low stocks, supply concerns and anxiety about whether Brazil may have a frost this year.
New York arabica futures vaulted to 34-month highs of $2.43 a lb basis July on Tuesday in a rally that has doubled prices since January.
London's futures for robusta type of beans hit a new one year-peak of $1,885 per tonne on Wednesday, up $68.
Lodder said official data from Brazil, the top grower, put the coming crop at 20 percent lower than this season.
"Colombia is also facing problems from excessive rains...so you will have a drop in production," he added. And roaster stocks were low.
"Roasters have to rely on prompt delivery of coffee and if you have a shortfall in supply next year, they have to be very careful on how to set up their programme of delivery."
Lodder said the current boom was part of the market cycle but the long-term price tendency was to move up or stay firm.
He also said that another phenomenon was the growth of internal consumption in the producing countries such as Brazil which could alter the supply balance.
The five-year time lag from planting decision to actual harvesting would mean trees to be planted this year in response to high prices would not yield crop until at least 2002.
"Of course the market will balance at the end of the day but at what level of price remains to be seen," Lodder said.
Lodder also gave a warning that retail coffee price increases above 40 percent could curtail consumption.
Several large U.S. and European roasters have put up retail prices by 20-30 percent in response to the rise in world prices.
